results.content: ￿hal-04667732￿ Evaluation methodology for disentangled uncertainty quantification on regression models Kevin Pasini 1, Clement Arlotti 1, Milad Leyli-abadi 1, Marc Nabhan 2 and Johanna Baro 1 * 1- IRT SystemX, Paris, France 2- Air Liquide, Les-Loges-en-Josas, France A practical way to enhance the confidence of the predictions made by Machine Learning (ML) models is to enrich them with trustworthiness add-ons such as Uncertainty Quantification (UQ). Existing UQ paradigms capture two intertwined components (epistemic and aleatoric), but few of them evalu-ate their disentanglement, even less on real data. We will first compare recent works on Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) regression in Machine Learning (ML), then propose a dUQ evaluation methodology based on a data withdrawal-based strategy that simulates OOD, aiming to assess the effective-ness of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty disentanglement. Table 1: Summary and comparison of UQ approaches > Features Problem support Environment setup Methods UQ paradigm Prior Decomposition UQ Regression Classification Dataset criteria Evaluation Interpretation Baselines [7] MCDP Drop-out No No Yes Yes (diverse) Public / Synthetic NLL / RMSE Local Yes (diverse) [9] DeepEnsemble Ensemble No No Yes Yes (stationary) Public / Synthetic Brier/Calibration NLL / RMSE Qualitative Local (diverse) Yes [6] AutoDEUQ Ensemble No Yes Yes No (stationary) Public / Synthetic NLL/RMSE No (diverse) Yes > [3] EDL Evidential Yes No Yes No (stationary) Public / Synthetic NLL/RMSE Quantitative Partial (diverse) Yes Color codes (green: satisfying, orange: partial, red: ignorance) 2 Disentangled Uncertainty Quantification framework To enable the cross-comparison and benchmarking of state-of-the-art approaches, we manipulate a UQ decomposition formalism to obtain a unified set of indica-tors. Experiment and evaluation In this section, we propose a set of experiments to evaluate the model epistemic confidence, despite the absence of ground truth by using a training data withdrawal strategy that simulate OOD data. 3 Experimental settings and results The benchmark compare four UQ paradigms on univariate time series: Random For-est disentangled Uncertainty Quantification (RF-dUQ)[1], Probabilistic Neural Net-work Monte Carlo Dropout (PNN-MCDP) [7], Probabilistic Neural Network Deep En-semble (PNN-DE)[9] and Evidential Deep Learning regression (EDL)[3]. Fig. 3: RF-UQ prediction with dUQ indicators from mid-var altered setup D-UQ evaluation synthesis: To ensure experimental robustness, 8 variants of the experiments (with 4 cross-validations) were performed on real and synthetic data.

results.title: Comparing robustness of MAE, MSE and RMSE | Towards Data Science
results.content: Usually the metrics used are the Mean Average Error (MAE), the Mean Squared Error (MSE) or the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE). This is done by the **MSE**, and higher errors (or distances) weigh more in the metric than lower ones, due to the nature of the power function. In this scenario it is easy to conclude that MSE may be less robust than MAE, since the squaring of the errors will enforce a higher importance on outliers. By changing the number of outliers (`num_outliers`) and the amplitude of the scalar by which we multiply the original observation point (`amplitude_outliers`), it is possible to compare the robustness of the metrics in many different scenarios. To conclude, now that it is clear the effects outliers can have in squared errors such as MSE or RMSE, it is important to say that in applications which are clear of noise these metrics can do more good than harm, since they can minimize greater errors even though it means accepting more frequent, smaller errors.

results.content: An archive of data science, data analytics, data engineering, machine learning, and artificial intelligence writing from the former Towards Data Science Medium publication. # Comparing Robustness of MAE, MSE and RMSE. If you deal with data, you probably already know that MSE is more sensitive to outliers than MAE. Usually the metrics used are the Mean Average Error (MAE), the Mean Squared Error (MSE) or the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE). This is done by the **MSE**, and higher errors (or distances) weigh more in the metric than lower ones, due to the nature of the power function. So a robust system or metric must be less affected by outliers. In this scenario it is easy to conclude that MSE may be less robust than MAE, since the squaring of the errors will enforce a higher importance on outliers. The goal here is to evaluate MAE, MSE and RMSE for each set of observations. By changing the number of outliers (`num_outliers`) and the amplitude of the scalar by which we multiply the original observation point (`amplitude_outliers`), it is possible to compare the robustness of the metrics in many different scenarios. evaluate_metrics(data, num_outliers = 0, amplitude_outliers = 1). But when taking the square root of the MSE and getting the RMSE we get a mean around 20, which is higher than the MAE. Also, the RMSE and MSE curves are identical, which is also expected, since the square root should not change the distribution, only the scale. evaluate_metrics(data, num_outliers = 2, amplitude_outliers = 2). Also, it is clear that the noisy MSE and RMSE distributions shifted more than the MAE ones. evaluate_metrics(data, num_outliers = 10, amplitude_outliers = 2). evaluate_metrics(data, num_outliers = 2, amplitude_outliers = 10). To conclude, now that it is clear the effects outliers can have in squared errors such as MSE or RMSE, it is important to say that in applications which are clear of noise these metrics can do more good than harm, since they can minimize greater errors even though it means accepting more frequent, smaller errors. ## Articles/Comparing robustness of MAE MSE and RMSE at main · vinyluis/Articles.

Title: Comparing Robustness of MAE, MSE and RMSE | by Vinícius Trevisan | TDS Archive | Medium
# Comparing Robustness of MAE, MSE and RMSE. If you deal with data, you probably already know that MSE is more sensitive to outliers than MAE. Usually the metrics used are the Mean Average Error (MAE), the Mean Squared Error (MSE) or the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE). This is done by the **MSE**, and higher errors (or distances) weigh more in the metric than lower ones, due to the nature of the power function. **RMSE** is used then to return the MSE error to the original unit by taking the square root of it, while maintaining the property of penalizing higher errors. So a robust system or metric must be less affected by outliers. In this scenario it is easy to conclude that MSE may be less robust than MAE, since the squaring of the errors will enforce a higher importance on outliers. The goal here is to evaluate MAE, MSE and RMSE for each set of observations. By changing the number of outliers (`num_outliers`) and the amplitude of the scalar by which we multiply the original observation point (`amplitude_outliers`), it is possible to compare the robustness of the metrics in many different scenarios. evaluate_metrics(data, num_outliers = 0, amplitude_outliers = 1). But when taking the square root of the MSE and getting the RMSE we get a mean around 20, which is higher than the MAE. Also, the RMSE and MSE curves are identical, which is also expected, since the square root should not change the distribution, only the scale. evaluate_metrics(data, num_outliers = 2, amplitude_outliers = 2). Also, it is clear that the noisy MSE and RMSE distributions shifted more than the MAE ones. evaluate_metrics(data, num_outliers = 10, amplitude_outliers = 2). evaluate_metrics(data, num_outliers = 2, amplitude_outliers = 10). To conclude, now that it is clear the effects outliers can have in squared errors such as MSE or RMSE, it is important to say that in applications which are clear of noise these metrics can do more good than harm, since they can minimize greater errors even though it means accepting more frequent, smaller errors. ## Articles/Comparing robustness of MAE MSE and RMSE at main · vinyluis/Articles.
